newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-BHP to end Newcastle steel making.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-BHP to end Newcastle steel making.

text.p: The Broken Hill Proprietary Co Ltd said on Tuesday that it would phase-out steel making at its major Newcastle plant north of Sydney by the end of 1999.
The company, Australia's largest, also said it planned to close its Geelong rod mill and Sydney wire mill in 1999.
Based on its review of domestic and international steel operations, BHP said it would disband its international steel division and restructure BHP Steel around four divisions.

BHP Steel chief executive Ron McNeilly said the group's year-long steel review had confirmed the world steel industry would continue to be intensely competitive with falling prices and new low capital intensive technologies.

"A reshaped Australian business with a strong focus on value-added downstream business supplying the building and construction markets of the Pacific Rim will position our steel business for the future," McNeilly said in a statement.
BHP said that although steelmaking would be phased out at Newcastle, the existing bar and rod mills would be expanded to form the nucleus of a rod, bar and wire business.
Feed for the Newcastle Mills would be produced at the Sydney Steel Mill and Whyalla Steelworks.
"The development of facilities at Whyalla to produce the required Newcastle feed will proceed immediately and they are expected to be operating in 1999," BHP said.
BHP's Sydney Wire mill would close during 1999, with further wire manufacturing capacity being installed at Newcastle, which would become the centre of BHP Steel's wire business.
"By the end of 1999, export business from Australasian plants will focus on added value flat products," BHP said.
Port Kembla Steelworks would continue its development as a flat products integrated steelworks with capacity rounded out to five million tonnes per annum by 1999, BHP said.

"Whyalla Steelworks will continue to operate at its current capacity of 1.2 million tonnes per annum supplying structurals and rails to the Australian market together with billets for the Newcastle rolling mills," BHP said.

BHP's steel despatches fell three percent to 4.185 million tonnes in the year to May 31, 1996, while raw steel production rose two percent to 8.624 million tonnes and marketable steel production fell one percent to 7.797 million tonnes.
BHP did not say in its statement how many of its over 3,000 workers would be laid off at Newcastle or how much such a restructuring would cost.

Organisationally BHP Steel will be restructured around four businesses. They are Integrated Steel Division, Coated Steel Division, Rod Bar and Wire Division and Buiding and Industrial Products Division.
BHP Steel's headquarters would remain in Melbourne.
"The four businesses will take full responsibility for their activities including international operations and growth, and concequently International Division will be disbanded," it said.
McNeilly said he recognised the restructuring would present difficulties.
"I especially regret the need to close steelmaking at Newcastle," he said.
"Newcastle was the company's entry point to steelmaking and the foundation from which we have built our presence in the industry," he said.
"Major industries have been built around this base and a great many people have contributed to the Works whilst also adding to the Newcastle community and its lifestyle."
BHP shares were up 17 cents at A$17.55 by 10.55 a.m. (0055 GMT).
